extracted.intended_audience: researchers applying for NSF grants, NSF program officers, and the science-policy community
extracted.subtask_description: A concise summary of changes to the National Science Foundation's merit-review process covering reviewer counts, panel usage, feedback verbosity, solicitations, program officer authority, and related National Science Board recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual Merit
rubrics_metrics.description: One of NSF's two long-standing review criteria used to judge proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditionally considered the primary criterion by many reviewers; the NSB report found that 61% of surveyed staff placed more weight on intellectual merit than on the second criterion. The report recommends ensuring intellectual merit is evaluated rigorously but balanced with societal considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader Impacts (aka Societal Benefits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The second of NSF's two long-standing review criteria, intended to capture the societal benefits of proposed research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NSB report recommends renaming this criterion to 'societal benefits' to clarify meaning and encourage equal consideration. The report also recommends reviewers go into more detail when rating this criterion because many reviewers give it short shrift. Examples of desired broader-impact activities include improving STEM education, improving public scientific literacy, and expanding participation in STEM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum number of outside (external) reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: NSF reduced the minimum number of outside expert reviews per proposal from three to two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reducing the number of external reviews is intended to improve efficiency but will shrink the influence of outside experts and increase the weight of program officer judgments. The NSB report cautions that fewer outside reviews may reduce the range of perspectives and expertise applied to each proposal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel review usage (panel optional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel review is now optional; program officers should assemble panels only when they want help making funding decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making panels optional aims to streamline processes, but fewer panels mean less group deliberation and reduced collective specialist input. The NSB report recommends seeking more outside perspectives rather than relying primarily on program officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program officer discretion and expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Program officers are given a larger role and encouraged to exercise more discretion in recommending proposals for funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With fewer external reviewers and optional panels, program officers' judgments will carry more weight. The NSB report questions whether program officers consistently have the necessary expertise to rate proposals on intellectual merit and societal benefits and recommends soliciting more outside expertise when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel summary length / feedback verbosity for rejected proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: New policy limits panel summaries for proposals to just three to five sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NSF frames shorter summaries as an efficiency measure. However, this reduces the amount of actionable feedback given to unsuccessful applicants and conflicts with the NSB recommendation for more detailed commentary, especially on the broader-impacts/societal-benefits criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and specificity of solicitations
rubrics_metrics.description: NSF will issue fewer—and broader—solicitations (calls for proposals) following organizational changes and staffing constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicitations historically provided detailed guidance on topic fit and were issued at the division level; eliminating divisions and issuing broader solicitations aims to encourage interdisciplinary work but gives applicants less granular guidance on whether a proposal is a good fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek input from a wider range of outside experts
rubrics_metrics.description: NSB recommends NSF seek input from more outside experts to provide a wider range of perspectives and expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recommendation is presented as a corrective to reduced external review and panel usage: more diverse external input can help identify important questions, urgent societal problems, and compensate for any gaps in program officer expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track and measure public benefits and agency risk aversion
rubrics_metrics.description: NSB recommends NSF do a better job of tracking how the public benefits from NSF grants and measure whether the agency is too conservative in tackling pressing societal issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementing such tracking would inform whether NSF's funding choices are meeting societal goals and whether the agency is avoiding higher-risk, higher-reward projects. Political sensitivities may complicate documentation of some projects' societal impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit inclusion of STEM education, public scientific literacy, and participation goals in broader impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The NSB report urges grantees and reviewers to pay attention to whether proposed research will improve STEM education, improve public scientific literacy, and expand participation in STEM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These activities are given as concrete examples of desirable societal benefits that should be integrated into proposals and evaluated with appropriate weight and detail in review comments.
